claim: Presenilin 1 (PS1) is an essential γ-secretase component responsible for amyloid precursor protein (APP) intramembraneous cleavage.
source: Presenilin 1 (PS1) is an essential γ-secretase component, the enzyme responsible for amyloid precursor protein (APP) intramembraneous cleavage.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PS1 function in the γ-secretase complex.

claim: Mutations in PS1 lead to dominant-inheritance of early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD).
source: Mutations in PS1 lead to dominant-inheritance of early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PS1 mutations and FAD inheritance patterns.

claim: Expression of FAD-linked PS1 mutations enhances toxic Aβ production.
source: Although expression of FAD-linked PS1 mutations enhances toxic Aβ production, the importance of other APP metabolites and γ-secretase substrates in the etiology of the disease has not been confirmed.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research on FAD-linked PS1 mutations.

claim: Neurons expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants exhibit enhanced axodendritic outgrowth due to increased levels of APP intracellular C-terminal fragment (APP-CTF).
source: We report that neurons expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants or functionally deficient PS1 exhibit enhanced axodendritic outgrowth due to increased levels of APP intracellular C-terminal fragment (APP-CTF).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons expressing functionally deficient PS1 exhibit enhanced axodendritic outgrowth due to increased levels of APP-CTF.
source: We report that neurons expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants or functionally deficient PS1 exhibit enhanced axodendritic outgrowth due to increased levels of APP intracellular C-terminal fragment (APP-CTF).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from PS1 KO and PS1 KI mice.

claim: APP expression is required for exuberant neurite outgrowth observed in knock-in mice expressing FAD-linked PS1 mutation.
source: APP expression is required for exuberant neurite outgrowth and hippocampal axonal sprouting observed in knock-in mice expressing FAD-linked PS1 mutation.
evidence: This is supported by data from APP KO x PS1 KI mice showing abolished neurite outgrowth.

claim: APP expression is required for hippocampal axonal sprouting observed in knock-in mice expressing FAD-linked PS1 mutation.
source: APP expression is required for exuberant neurite outgrowth and hippocampal axonal sprouting observed in knock-in mice expressing FAD-linked PS1 mutation.
evidence: This is supported by GAP-43 staining data in PS1 KI and APP KO x PS1 KI mice.

claim: APP-CTF accumulation initiates CREB signaling cascade through an association of APP-CTF with Gαs protein.
source: APP-CTF accumulation initiates CREB signaling cascade through an association of APP-CTF with Gαs protein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased pCREB levels and the effect of adenylate cyclase inhibition.

claim: Pathological PS1 loss-of-function impinges on neurite formation through a selective APP gain-of-function.
source: We demonstrate that pathological PS1 loss-of-function impinges on neurite formation through a selective APP gain-of-function that could impact on axodendritic connectivity and contribute to aberrant axonal sprouting observed in AD patients.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: A mutation in presenilin genes causes autosomal dominant early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD).
source: A mutation in presenilin genes causes autosomal dominant early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD) (Tanzi and Bertram, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tanzi and Bertram, 2001.

claim: PS1 acts as the catalytic core of the multisubunit γ-secretase complex.
source: Gene knockout studies in mice reveal that PS1 acts as the catalytic core of the multisubunit γ-secretase complex that is responsible for regulated intramembranous proteolysis of several type-I transmembrane protein substrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge from gene knockout studies in mice.

claim: Over 90 substrates of γ-secretase have been identified including APP, Notch, Eph receptors and ligands, cadherins, and DCC.
source: Over 90 substrates have been identified so far including amyloid precursor protein (APP), Notch and Eph receptors and ligands, cadherins, and deleted in colorectal cancer (DCC) (Haapasalo and Kovacs, 2011; Kopan and Ilagan, 2004; McCarthy et al., 2009; Parks and Curtis, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Cleavage of full-length APP by α- or β-secretases releases the entire ectodomain leaving behind membrane-bound C-terminal fragments (APP-C83 and APP-C99, respectively).
source: Therefore, cleavage of full-length APP (APP-FL) by α- or β-secretases releases the entire ectodomain (soluble APPα or soluble APPβ, respectively), leaving behind membrane-bound C-terminal fragments (CTF), comprising the transmembrane and cytoplasmic domain (APP-C83 and APP-C99, respectively).
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing pathways.

claim: Subsequent cleavage of APP-CTF by γ-secretase releases the cytosolic domain from the membrane (AICD) and either p3 fragment or the neurotoxic Aβ peptide.
source: Subsequent cleavage of APP-CTF by γ-secretase releases the cytosolic domain from the membrane (APP intracellular domain, AICD) and either p3 fragment or the neurotoxic Aβ peptide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APP processing by γ-secretase.

claim: Inhibiting γ-secretase activity prevents accumulation of Aβ and AICD in favor of accumulation of APP-C83 or APP-C99.
source: Consequently, inhibiting γ-secretase activity would prevent accumulation of Aβ and AICD in favor of accumulation of APP-C83 or APP-C99 depending on their prior non-amylogenic α-CTF or amylogenic β-CTF cleavage products, respectively.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the established APP processing pathway.

claim: Accumulation of APP-CTF in the raft produces a marked increase of neurite extension in cortical neurons.
source: We previously demonstrated that accumulation of APP-CTF in the raft produced a marked increase of neurite extension in a variety of neuronal cells including cortical neurons (Deyts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Overexpression of APP and concurrent γ-secretase inhibition leads to an increase in neurite outgrowth.
source: We also observed that overexpression of APP and concurrent γ-secretase inhibition, that produce an accumulation of APP-CTF and other γ-secretase-dependent CTF substrates, leads to an increase in neurite outgrowth (Deyts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Lack of APP expression modestly but significantly and selectively alters axonal outgrowth.
source: Lack of APP expression modestly (but significantly) and selectively altered axonal outgrowth (Figure 1b1; WT, 1.00 ± 0.03; APP KO, 0.77 ± 0.05, P<0.001), whereas the dendritic outgrowth was not affected (Figure 1b2, see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from APP KO neurons shown in Figure 1.

claim: Dendritic outgrowth is not affected by lack of APP expression.
source: Lack of APP expression modestly (but significantly) and selectively altered axonal outgrowth (Figure 1b1; WT, 1.00 ± 0.03; APP KO, 0.77 ± 0.05, P<0.001), whereas the dendritic outgrowth was not affected (Figure 1b2, see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from APP KO neurons shown in Figure 1.

claim: Inhibition of γ-secretase in WT neurons enhances axonal and dendritic outgrowth.
source: We observed that inhibition of γ-secretase in WT neurons enhances axonal and dendritic outgrowth (Figure 1b1 and b2), with a more predominant effect on the axon as reflected by an increase of the axon/dendrite area ratio (see Figure 1b3; WT, 1.78 ± 0.07; WT+CompE, 2.52 ± 0.18, P< 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using Compound E treatment shown in Figure 1.

claim: γ-secretase inhibition has a more predominant effect on axonal outgrowth compared to dendritic outgrowth.
source: We observed that inhibition of γ-secretase in WT neurons enhances axonal and dendritic outgrowth (Figure 1b1 and b2), with a more predominant effect on the axon as reflected by an increase of the axon/dendrite area ratio (see Figure 1b3; WT, 1.78 ± 0.07; WT+CompE, 2.52 ± 0.18, P< 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by the axon/dendrite ratio data shown in Figure 1b3.

claim: Neurons treated with γ-secretase inhibitor do not exhibit axonal or dendritic outgrowth in the absence of APP expression.
source: Interestingly, we observed that neurons treated with γ-secretase inhibitor did not exhibit axonal or dendritic outgrowth in the absence of APP expression (Figure 1b1 and b2), suggesting that APP is the main contributing factor in γ-secretase-mediated neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from APP KO neurons treated with Compound E shown in Figure 1.

claim: APP is the main contributing factor in γ-secretase-mediated neurite outgrowth.
source: Interestingly, we observed that neurons treated with γ-secretase inhibitor did not exhibit axonal or dendritic outgrowth in the absence of APP expression (Figure 1b1 and b2), suggesting that APP is the main contributing factor in γ-secretase-mediated neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that γ-secretase inhibition does not affect neurite outgrowth in APP KO neurons.

claim: Inhibition of γ-secretase activity produces an overall increase of APP-CTF whereas APP-FL is not changed.
source: In our neuronal cultures, fractionation of lysates on Tris-Tricine gels showed that the inhibition of γ-secretase activity produced an overall increase of APP-CTF whereas APP-FL was not changed (Figure 1c2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1c2.

claim: γ-secretase dependent processing of APP affects accumulation of both APP-CTFα and APP-CTFβ in HEK293 and COS-7 cells.
source: As expected, we confirmed that γ-secretase dependent processing of APP affects accumulation of both APP-CTFα and APP-CTFβ, at least in HEK293 and COS-7 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of APP-FL is not sufficient to induce axodendritic outgrowth.
source: Overexpression of APP-FL was not sufficient to induce axodendritic outgrowth, although accumulation of APP-CTF through γ-secretase inhibition did promote axodendritic outgrowth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Accumulation of APP-CTF through γ-secretase inhibition promotes axodendritic outgrowth.
source: Overexpression of APP-FL was not sufficient to induce axodendritic outgrowth, although accumulation of APP-CTF through γ-secretase inhibition did promote axodendritic outgrowth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Inhibition of γ-secretase activity favors a preferential augmentation of axonal outgrowth in comparison to the dendritic compartment.
source: This set of data confirmed that inhibition of γ-secretase activity favors a preferential augmentation of axonal outgrowth in comparison to the dendritic compartment, as shown by the increase of the axon/dendrite ratio (Figure 1b3).
evidence: This is supported by the axon/dendrite ratio data shown in Figure 1b3.

claim: Axodendritic outgrowth and associated signaling are reversed in the absence of APP expression.
source: This effect was abolished in the absence of endogenous APP expression and restored by APP overexpression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from APP KO neurons with and without APP overexpression.

claim: Both γ-secretase inhibition and APP expression are required to induce axodendritic outgrowth.
source: Our findings emphasize that both γ-secretase inhibition and APP expression are required to induce axodendritic outgrowth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the requirement of both factors.

claim: Inhibition of γ-secretase activity or lack of presenilin 1 expression produces an endogenous accumulation of APP-CTF in the brain, neuronal cultures, or cell lines.
source: It is well established that inhibition of γ-secretase activity, or lack of presenilin 1 (PS1) expression, produces an endogenous accumulation of APP-CTF in the brain, neuronal cultures, or cell lines (Bentahir et al., 2006; De Strooper et al., 1998; Parent et al., 2005; Walker et al., 2005; Woodruff et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Expression of FAD-linked PS1 mutant proteins may attenuate γ-secretase activity, consequently limiting proteolysis of full-length protein substrates and accumulating their CTF.
source: In earlier studies, it has been proposed that expression of FAD-linked PS1 mutant proteins may attenuate γ-secretase activity, consequently limiting proteolysis of full-length protein substrates and, therefore, accumulating their CTF (Bentahir et al., 2006; De Strooper, 2007; Shen and Kelleher, 2007; Walker et al., 2005; Wolfe, 2007; Woodruff et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: APP-CTF accumulates in PS1 mutants compared to PS1-WT.
source: We observed that APP-CTF accumulates in PS1 mutants, as compared to PS1-WT (Figure 2a2), confirming previous findings that pathogenic PS1 mutations might reduce γ-secretase activity (Bentahir et al., 2006; De Strooper, 2007; Heilig et al., 2013; Shen and Kelleher, 2007; Walker et al., 2005; Woodruff et al., 2013; Xia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2a2 and citations to prior research.

claim: Neurons expressing PS1-ΔE9 mutation exhibit a significant increase in axodendritic outgrowth.
source: Interestingly, we observed that neurons expressing PS1-ΔE9 mutation exhibit a significant increase in axodendritic outgrowth (Figure 2b and c), an effect that is exacerbated by the presence of APP-FL in neurons overexpressing PS1-M146L and PS1-D385A mutations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: The effect of PS1-ΔE9 mutation on axodendritic outgrowth is exacerbated by the presence of APP-FL in neurons overexpressing PS1-M146L and PS1-D385A mutations.
source: Interestingly, we observed that neurons expressing PS1-ΔE9 mutation exhibit a significant increase in axodendritic outgrowth (Figure 2b and c), an effect that is exacerbated by the presence of APP-FL in neurons overexpressing PS1-M146L and PS1-D385A mutations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: Pathogenic PS1 mutations favor axodendritic outgrowth as seen under a condition that reduces γ-secretase activity.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that pathogenic PS1 mutations favor axodendritic outgrowth as seen under a condition that reduces γ-secretase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on PS1 mutations.

claim: Western blot analysis of steady-state APP expression levels in brains of E15 mouse embryos reveals a significant increase of APP-CTFα in PS1 KI.
source: As shown in Figure 3a, Western blot analysis of steady-state APP expression levels in brains of E15 mouse embryos reveals a significant increase of APP-CTFα in PS1 KI, and larger increase of both APP-CTFα and APP-CTFβ in PS1 KO as compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Western blot analysis of steady-state APP expression levels in brains of E15 mouse embryos reveals a larger increase of both APP-CTFα and APP-CTFβ in PS1 KO compared to WT.
source: As shown in Figure 3a, Western blot analysis of steady-state APP expression levels in brains of E15 mouse embryos reveals a significant increase of APP-CTFα in PS1 KI, and larger increase of both APP-CTFα and APP-CTFβ in PS1 KO as compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: APP-CTF increases similarly in total membrane fractions of heterozygous (PS1 KI/+) and homozygous (PS1 KI/KI) brains harvested during synaptogenesis (postnatal day 10) compared to WT littermates.
source: Analysis of brain lysates revealed similar increases of APP-CTF in total membrane fractions of heterozygous (PS1 KI/+) and homozygous (PS1 KI/KI) brains harvested during synaptogenesis (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a1, postnatal day 10 – P10) or in adulthood (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; 6 months-old – 6M), as compared to their WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: APP-CTF increases similarly in total membrane fractions of heterozygous (PS1 KI/+) and homozygous (PS1 KI/KI) brains harvested in adulthood (6 months-old) compared to WT littermates.
source: Analysis of brain lysates revealed similar increases of APP-CTF in total membrane fractions of heterozygous (PS1 KI/+) and homozygous (PS1 KI/KI) brains harvested during synaptogenesis (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a1, postnatal day 10 – P10) or in adulthood (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; 6 months-old – 6M), as compared to their WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Levels of APP-FL are not significantly affected among PS1 KI groups.
source: Levels of APP-FL were not significantly affected among these groups (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Ratios of APP-CTF/APP-FL are increased in PS1 KI brains.
source: Consequently, ratios of APP-CTF/APP-FL were increased in PS1 KI brains (Figure 3b2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b2), suggesting that the FAD-linked PS1 mutation may result in loss of activity toward APP proteolysis, leading to accumulation of membrane-tethered APP-CTF.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3b2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b2.

claim: The FAD-linked PS1 mutation may result in loss of activity toward APP proteolysis, leading to accumulation of membrane-tethered APP-CTF.
source: Consequently, ratios of APP-CTF/APP-FL were increased in PS1 KI brains (Figure 3b2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b2), suggesting that the FAD-linked PS1 mutation may result in loss of activity toward APP proteolysis, leading to accumulation of membrane-tethered APP-CTF.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased APP-CTF/APP-FL ratio data.

claim: APP-CTF accumulates to a lesser extent in PS1 KI compared to PS1 KO.
source: However, APP-CTF accumulated to a lesser extent in PS1 KI as compared to PS1 KO (Figure 3a), therefore supporting the notion of partial loss-of-function mutant.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: PS1 KI represents a partial loss-of-function mutant.
source: However, APP-CTF accumulated to a lesser extent in PS1 KI as compared to PS1 KO (Figure 3a), therefore supporting the notion of partial loss-of-function mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of APP-CTF accumulation between PS1 KI and PS1 KO.

claim: Primary cortical neurons generated from PS1 KO and PS1 KI mice exhibit exuberant axodendritic outgrowth.
source: We observed that primary cortical neurons generated from PS1 KO and PS1 KI mice harboring the FAD-linked PS1-M146V variant exhibit exuberant axodendritic outgrowth (see summarized results in Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c and d and summarized in Table 1.

claim: Primary cortical neurons generated from PS1 KO and PS1 KI mice exhibit a significant increase in both axonal and dendritic outgrowth compared to WT.
source: We observed a significant increase in both axonal and dendritic outgrowth in PS1 KI cultured neurons as compared to WT, an effect as substantial as the effect seen in neurons lacking PS1 expression (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Axonal and dendritic outgrowth is increased without apparent bias toward either neuronal compartment in PS1 KI neurons.
source: Axonal and dendritic outgrowth was increased without apparent bias toward either neuronal compartment.
evidence: This is observed from the quantitative data in Figure 3d showing similar increases in both compartments.

claim: PS1 mutation-induced neurite outgrowth is comparable in neurons expressing one or two copies of the mutated gene.
source: Strikingly, we noticed that PS1 mutation-induced neurite outgrowth was comparable in neurons expressing one or two copies of the mutated gene, which is consistent with the idea of autosomal dominant inheritance of PSEN1 mutations.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing heterozygous and homozygous PS1 KI neurons.

claim: Modest reduction in γ-secretase activity through an endogenous level of PS1 mutation expression is sufficient to influence drastically axodendritic outgrowth.
source: Our findings also suggest that modest reduction in γ-secretase activity through an endogenous level of PS1 mutation expression is sufficient to influence drastically axodendritic outgrowth, an effect that emerges in conjunction with modest APP-CTF accumulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that even heterozygous PS1 KI neurons show substantial neurite outgrowth.

claim: Lack of APP expression abolishes excess axonal and dendritic outgrowth found in neurons carrying the PS1-M146V mutation.
source: Remarkably, lack of APP expression abolished excess axonal and dendritic outgrowth found in neurons carrying the PS1-M146V mutation (Figure 3d1; 97% and 62% reduction, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from APP KO x PS1 KI neurons shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Presenilin-dependent enhancement of axodendritic outgrowth is not further increased in APP KO x PS1 KI cultures treated with γ-secretase inhibitor.
source: We observed that presenilin-dependent enhancement of axodendritic outgrowth was not furthermore increased in APP KO x PS1 KI cultures (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), supporting the idea that APP is the major contributing substrate in FAD-linked PS1 mutation induced neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: APP is the major contributing substrate in FAD-linked PS1 mutation induced neurite outgrowth.
source: We observed that presenilin-dependent enhancement of axodendritic outgrowth was not furthermore increased in APP KO x PS1 KI cultures (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), supporting the idea that APP is the major contributing substrate in FAD-linked PS1 mutation induced neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additional effect of γ-secretase inhibition in APP KO x PS1 KI neurons.

claim: γ-secretase-dependent accumulation of DCC-CTF promotes neurite outgrowth in neuroblastoma cells.
source: We and others have previously reported that γ-secretase-dependent accumulation of Deleted Colorectal Cancer C-terminal fragment (DCC-CTF) promotes neurite outgrowth in neuroblastoma cells (Parent et al., 2005) and motor neuron explants (Bai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: γ-secretase-dependent accumulation of DCC-CTF promotes neurite outgrowth in motor neuron explants.
source: We and others have previously reported that γ-secretase-dependent accumulation of Deleted Colorectal Cancer C-terminal fragment (DCC-CTF) promotes neurite outgrowth in neuroblastoma cells (Parent et al., 2005) and motor neuron explants (Bai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Lack of DCC expression does not affect axonal or dendritic outgrowth in primary neuron culture system.
source: We observed that lack of DCC expression does not affect axonal or dendritic outgrowth in our cell culture system (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from DCC KO neurons shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: Enhancement of axodendritic outgrowth is similar in naïve WT and DCC KO neurons treated with γ-secretase inhibitor.
source: Within the same experimental conditions, sets of neurons were treated with γ-secretase inhibitor Compound E to abrogate substrate proteolysis. In these groups, enhancement of axodendritic outgrowth was similar in naïve WT as compared to DCC KO neurons treated with a γ-secretase inhibitor (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lack of DCC expression does not affect axodendritic outgrowth in neurons expressing FAD-linked PS1-M146V mutation.
source: We also confirmed that lack of DCC expression did not affect axodendritic outgrowth in neurons expressing FAD-linked PS1-M146V mutation (Figure 3c and d), even though DCC-CTF was increased in cultured neuron lysates of homozygous and heterozygote PS1 KI relative to WT (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from DCC KO x PS1 KI neurons shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: DCC-CTF is increased in cultured neuron lysates of homozygous and heterozygote PS1 KI relative to WT.
source: We also confirmed that lack of DCC expression did not affect axodendritic outgrowth in neurons expressing FAD-linked PS1-M146V mutation (Figure 3c and d), even though DCC-CTF was increased in cultured neuron lysates of homozygous and heterozygote PS1 KI relative to WT (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: DCC-CTF increase is significant in vivo during early brain development and the period of synaptogenesis (E15-P14) in PS1 KI mice compared to WT.
source: An increase of DCC-CTF detection was also significant in vivo during early brain development and the period of synaptogenesis (E15-P14) in PS1 KI mice as compared to WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: DCC is not an essential substrate for γ-secretase induced neurite outgrowth.
source: Therefore, our results indicate that DCC is not an essential substrate for γ-secretase induced neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of effect of DCC deletion on neurite outgrowth in various conditions.

claim: GAP-43 staining correlates selectively with axonal development and is prominent in brain areas where axon fibers project.
source: As observed by several groups (Benowitz et al., 1988; Goslin et al., 1988; Oestreicher and Gispen, 1986), GAP-43 staining correlates selectively with axonal development and is prominent in brain areas where axon fibers project.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: GAP-43 expression is significantly increased in hippocampal areas of PS1 KI mice.
source: Consistent with our neurite outgrowth analysis, GAP-43 expression is significantly increased in hippocampal areas of PS1 KI mice, an effect that was abrogated if APP expression was absent (see Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Increased GAP-43 expression in PS1 KI mice is abrogated if APP expression is absent.
source: Consistent with our neurite outgrowth analysis, GAP-43 expression is significantly increased in hippocampal areas of PS1 KI mice, an effect that was abrogated if APP expression was absent (see Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data from APP KO x PS1 KI mice shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Intensity of GAP-43 immunostaining is selectively increased in the stratum lacunosum moleculare (LMol) and the outer and inner molecular layers of the dentate gyrus (OMoDG and IMoDG) in PS1 KI mice compared to WT.
source: Quantitative analysis reveals that intensity of GAP-43 immunostaining was selectively increased in the stratum lacunosum moleculare (LMol) and the outer and inner molecular layers of the dentate gyrus (OMoDG and IMoDG, respectively) in PS1 KI mice as compared to WT (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: GAP-43 expression is increased in the hippocampus as early as postnatal day 10 (P10) in PS1 KI compared to APP KO x PS1 KI mice.
source: We confirmed by Western blot analysis that GAP-43 expression was increased as well in the hippocampus as early as at postnatal day 10 (P10) in PS1 KI as compared to APP KO x PS1 KI mice, an effect that was not observed in the cortex of these mice (Figures 4b and c).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 4b and c.

claim: Increased GAP-43 expression in PS1 KI is not observed in the cortex.
source: We confirmed by Western blot analysis that GAP-43 expression was increased as well in the hippocampus as early as at postnatal day 10 (P10) in PS1 KI as compared to APP KO x PS1 KI mice, an effect that was not observed in the cortex of these mice (Figures 4b and c).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 4b and c.

claim: Mice expressing an endogenous level of FAD-linked PS1 variant exhibit exuberant neurite outgrowth and axonal sprouting at close proximity to the perforant path, which requires APP expression.
source: Altogether, our results indicate that mice expressing an endogenous level of FAD-linked PS1 variant exhibit exuberant neurite outgrowth and axonal sprouting at close proximity to the perforant path, which requires APP expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GAP-43 staining and neurite outgrowth data.

claim: Concomitant expression of APP-FL and inhibition of γ-secretase activity favors neurite outgrowth in cortical neuronal cultures.
source: As described in our previous studies (Deyts et al., 2012) and shown in Figure 5, we observed that concomitant expression of APP-FL and inhibition of γ-secretase activity favors neurite outgrowth (Figure 5a) and associated increase of phosphorylated CREB (pCREB, Figure 5b) in cortical neuronal cultures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a and b.

claim: Concomitant expression of APP-FL and inhibition of γ-secretase activity is associated with an increase of phosphorylated CREB (pCREB) in cortical neuronal cultures.
source: As described in our previous studies (Deyts et al., 2012) and shown in Figure 5, we observed that concomitant expression of APP-FL and inhibition of γ-secretase activity favors neurite outgrowth (Figure 5a) and associated increase of phosphorylated CREB (pCREB, Figure 5b) in cortical neuronal cultures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Neurons overexpressing APP-C99 exhibit increased axodendritic outgrowth.
source: In support of this finding, we also observed that neurons overexpressing APP-C99 (the APP β-secretase cleaved CTF by-product) exhibit increased axodendritic outgrowth that was prevented by the expression of a C99 construct lacking the GαS-protein interacting site where three alanine substitutions were introduced to replace the basic residues of the BBXXB motif in APP-CTF (named C99mutAAA; see Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Increased axodendritic outgrowth in neurons overexpressing APP-C99 is prevented by expression of a C99 construct lacking the GαS-protein interacting site (C99mutAAA).
source: In support of this finding, we also observed that neurons overexpressing APP-C99 (the APP β-secretase cleaved CTF by-product) exhibit increased axodendritic outgrowth that was prevented by the expression of a C99 construct lacking the GαS-protein interacting site where three alanine substitutions were introduced to replace the basic residues of the BBXXB motif in APP-CTF (named C99mutAAA; see Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Neurons expressing APP-C99 or mAICD constructs exhibit a strong increase of CREB signaling illustrated by the enhancement of pCREB immunostaining.
source: As shown in Figure 5b, we observed that neurons expressing APP-C99 or mAICD constructs exhibit a strong increase of CREB signaling illustrated by the enhancement of pCREB immunostaining.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Enhanced pCREB immunostaining in neurons expressing APP-C99 or mAICD is abolished in neurons overexpressing mutants lacking GαS-protein interacting site (C99mutAAA and mAICDmutAAA).
source: These outcomes were abolished in neurons overexpressing mutant lacking GαS-protein interacting site C99mutAAA and mAICDmutAAA, respectively (Figure 5b1 and b2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: CREB signaling effects are more noticeable in the somatic/nuclear area compared to dendritic projections.
source: As expected for CREB signaling, these effects are more noticeable in the somatic/nuclear area as compared to dendritic projections (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither sAPPα nor sAPPβ overexpression influences CREB signaling in HEK293 cells or in neurons lacking APP expression.
source: We observed that neither sAPPα nor sAPPβ overexpression influenced CREB signaling in HEK293 cells or in neurons lacking APP expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a and Figure 5c1, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a and Figure 5c1.

claim: Increase in APP-CTF accumulation causes changes in neurite outgrowth and CREB signaling in PS1 loss-of-function neurons.
source: Altogether, our results point out that increase in APP-CTF accumulation is causing changes in neurite outgrowth and CREB signaling in PS1 loss-of-function neurons, therefore supporting the idea that APP-CTF accumulation is the main contributing factor to PS1-dependent modulation of CREB signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on APP-CTF and CREB signaling.

claim: APP-CTF accumulation is the main contributing factor to PS1-dependent modulation of CREB signaling.
source: Altogether, our results point out that increase in APP-CTF accumulation is causing changes in neurite outgrowth and CREB signaling in PS1 loss-of-function neurons, therefore supporting the idea that APP-CTF accumulation is the main contributing factor to PS1-dependent modulation of CREB signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Primary cortical neurons generated from PS1 KI mice exhibit a significant overall increase of phosphorylated PKA substrates.
source: We observed that primary cortical neurons generated from PS1 KI mice exhibit a significant overall increase of phosphorylated PKA substrates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Associated PKA-dependent CREB signaling is substantiated by an increase in pCREB immunostaining in PS1 KI neurons compared to WT littermates.
source: Associated PKA-dependent CREB signaling was substantiated by an increase in pCREB immunostaining as compared to their WT littermates (Figure 6a1 and a2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Neurons lacking PS1 function exhibit increased pCREB levels.
source: As we have described previously (Barnes et al., 2008), we reiterate here that neurons lacking PS1 function exhibit increased pCREB levels (Figure 6a2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6a2 and citation to prior work.

claim: pCREB is significantly increased in neuron lysates generated from PS1 KI mice.
source: We confirmed by Western blot analysis that pCREB was significantly increased in neuron lysates generated from PS1 KI mice (Figure 6b1 and b3), an effect that was also reported in neuroblastoma cell lines and mouse brains expressing FAD-linked PS1 mutations (Muller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6b1 and b3 and citation to prior research.

claim: pCREB levels are increased in neurons treated with γ-secretase inhibitor or neurons generated from PS1 KO mouse brains.
source: In line with PS1 loss-of-function phenotype, Western blot analysis of neuronal lysates confirmed increases of pCREB levels in neurons treated with γ-secretase inhibitor or neurons generated from PS1 KO mouse brains (Figure 6b2 and b3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6b2 and b3.

claim: Neurons generated from APP KO present a significant decrease in pCREB level.
source: In support of our neurite outgrowth studies presented in Figure 1, we likewise observed that neurons generated from APP KO present a significant decrease in pCREB level (Figure 6a2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6a2.

claim: Neurons generated from PS1 KI mice that lack APP expression (APP KO x PS1 KI) do not show increased pCREB as observed in PS1 KI littermates.
source: More interestingly, we found that neurons generated from PS1 KI mice that lack APP expression (APP KO x PS1 KI) do not show increased pCREB as observed in PS1 KI littermates, an effect that was not seen in neurons lacking DCC expression (Figure 6a1, a2, b2, and b3).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Neurons lacking DCC expression show increased pCREB in PS1 KI background.
source: More interestingly, we found that neurons generated from PS1 KI mice that lack APP expression (APP KO x PS1 KI) do not show increased pCREB as observed in PS1 KI littermates, an effect that was not seen in neurons lacking DCC expression (Figure 6a1, a2, b2, and b3).
evidence: This is supported by data from DCC KO x PS1 KI neurons shown in Figure 6.

claim: APP expression is associated with the increase in CREB signaling in PS1 KI neurons.
source: Therefore, we conclude that APP expression is associated with the increase in CREB signaling in PS1 KI neurons.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that APP deletion abolishes increased CREB signaling in PS1 KI neurons.

claim: APP is sufficient and necessary to induce CREB signaling in the loss-of-function PS1 mutant.
source: Our results confirm that APP is sufficient and necessary to induce CREB signaling in the loss-of-function PS1 mutant (see summary Table 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: Adenylate cyclase inhibition profoundly reduces CREB activity in neurons generated from PS1 KI.
source: We observed that adenylate cyclase inhibition profoundly reduced CREB activity in neurons generated from PS1 KI.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using MDL-12,330A treatment shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Enhanced neurite outgrowth in neurons expressing PS1 mutants is dependent on adenylate cyclase activity.
source: We also confirmed that enhanced neurite outgrowth in neurons expressing PS1 mutants was dependent on adenylate cyclase activity (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using MDL-12,330A treatment shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Neurons generated from transgenic mice coexpressing APPswe and PS1-ΔE9 mutations (Tg85Dbo) exhibit a significant increase of axodendritic outgrowth compared to non-transgenic littermates.
source: We generated cortical neuronal cultures from transgenic mouse embryos coexpressing APPswe and PS1-ΔE9 mutations (Tg85Dbo), a mouse model associated with accumulation of Aβ burden (Jankowsky et al., 2005). We observed a significant increase of axodendritic outgrowth in Tg85Dbo as compared to their non-transgenic littermates, at the same level seen in neurons generated from PS1 KO and PS1 KI (Figure 7b2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b2.

claim: Increased axodendritic outgrowth in Tg85Dbo neurons is completely alleviated by 24 hr treatment with adenylate cyclase inhibitor.
source: This effect was completely alleviated by a 24 hr treatment with adenylate cyclase inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using MDL-12,330A treatment shown in Figure 7b.

claim: cAMP/PKA-dependent signaling is required to induce neurite outgrowth in neurons that exhibit increased APP-CTF.
source: Altogether, our results confirm the requirement of cAMP/PKA-dependent signaling to induce neurite outgrowth in neurons that exhibit increased APP-CTF (see summary Table 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the adenylate cyclase inhibition experiments.

claim: APP is not an important contributing factor to neurite formation under normal physiological condition.
source: Our investigations point out that APP is not an important contributing factor to neurite formation under normal physiological condition.
evidence: This is inferred from the modest effect of APP deletion on axonal outgrowth under basal conditions.

claim: Loss of APP expression only slightly affects axonal outgrowth in cell culture system.
source: In fact, loss of APP expression only slightly affects axonal outgrowth, at least in cell culture system.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from APP KO neurons.

claim: APP KO mice are viable.
source: APP KO mice are viable (Zheng et al., 1995), and present subtle, age-dependent decline in memory tasks (Ring et al., 2007; Schrenk-Siemens et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: APP KO mice present subtle, age-dependent decline in memory tasks.
source: APP KO mice are viable (Zheng et al., 1995), and present subtle, age-dependent decline in memory tasks (Ring et al., 2007; Schrenk-Siemens et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: γ-secretase-dependent inhibition of APP processing and subsequent APP-CTF accumulation mediates a striking impact on axodendritic growth.
source: Nonetheless, our study clearly indicates that γ-secretase-dependent inhibition of APP processing, and subsequent APP-CTF accumulation, mediates a striking impact on axodendritic growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data throughout the study.

claim: Among all known γ-secretase substrates, APP is the key contributing substrate in observed dysregulation of neurite outgrowth.
source: It appears that among all known (and unknown) γ-secretase substrates, APP is the key contributing substrate in observed dysregulation of neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of APP and DCC deletion effects on neurite outgrowth.

claim: Exuberant axonal sprouting observed in adult PS1 KI mice selectively affects hippocampal areas connected with entorhinal cortex/perforant path projections.
source: Noteworthy, the exuberant axonal sprouting observed in adult PS1 KImice selectively affects the hippocampal areas that are connected with entorhinal cortex/perforant path projections (Forster et al., 2006), which is reminiscent of the aberrant sprouting described in AD patients (Arendt, 2001; Geddes et al., 1985; Masliah et al., 1991; Rekart et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by GAP-43 staining data and citations to prior research.

claim: Exuberant axonal sprouting in PS1 KI mice is reminiscent of aberrant sprouting described in AD patients.
source: Noteworthy, the exuberant axonal sprouting observed in adult PS1 KImice selectively affects the hippocampal areas that are connected with entorhinal cortex/perforant path projections (Forster et al., 2006), which is reminiscent of the aberrant sprouting described in AD patients (Arendt, 2001; Geddes et al., 1985; Masliah et al., 1991; Rekart et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on AD patients.

claim: Higher intensity levels of GAP-43 correlate with hippocampal sprouting in the molecular layer in mouse model overexpressing FAD-linked APP variant.
source: Higher intensity levels of GAP-43 correlated with the hippocampal sprouting in the molecular layer seen in mouse model overexpressing the FAD-linked APP variant (Chin et al., 2004; Phinney et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Lack of APP expression in rodent or Drosophila models can lead to inaccuracies in axon guidance in some parts of the brain, including commissural projections.
source: Clearly, it has been reported that lack of APP expression in rodent or Drosophila models could lead to inaccuracies in axon guidance in some parts of the brain, including the commissural projections (Magara et al., 1999; Rama et al., 2012) and mushroom body development, a Drosophila brain structure involved in learning and memory (Soldano et al., 2013) [see also (Muller and Zheng, 2012; Nicolas and Hassan, 2014) for review].
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Drosophila lacking APP homolog expression requires the APP-CTF component for accurate axonal outgrowth.
source: More interestingly, Drosophila lacking the APP homolog expression requires the APP-CTF component for accurate axonal outgrowth (Soldano et al., 2013), indicating the significance of APP-CTF for proper axonal guidance and memory function in Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: CREB signaling is important for memory consolidation and cellular events that preserve cell integrity.
source: It is widely accepted that CREB signaling is important for memory consolidation and cellular events that preserve cell integrity [review by (Abel and Nguyen, 2008; Alberini and Kandel, 2015; Lonze and Ginty, 2002)].
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Ablation of CREB is associated with axonal and dendritic outgrowth defects.
source: Conversely, ablation of CREB is associated with axonal and dendritic outgrowth defects (Lonze et al., 2002; Redmond et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Long-term synaptic plasticity is enhanced in several mouse models expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants.
source: Even though long-term synaptic plasticity is enhanced in several mouse models expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants (Parent et al., 1999; Parent and Thinakaran, 2010), which is consistent with an increase in CREB signaling, a number of these mice performed poorly in a variety of memory tasks (Webster et al., 2014; Xia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mouse models expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants performed poorly in a variety of memory tasks.
source: Even though long-term synaptic plasticity is enhanced in several mouse models expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants (Parent et al., 1999; Parent and Thinakaran, 2010), which is consistent with an increase in CREB signaling, a number of these mice performed poorly in a variety of memory tasks (Webster et al., 2014; Xia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increase of CREB signaling in cell lines and brain lysates from mouse lines carrying PS1 mutations can be reversed or normalized by interfering with ER Ca2+ stores and the IP3-dependent signaling pathway.
source: An increase of CREB signaling, in cell lines and brain lysates generated from mouse lines carrying PS1 mutations (including the PS1M146V mutation), can be reversed or normalized by interfering with ER Ca2+ stores and the IP3-dependent signaling pathway, an effect that eliminated Aβ toxicity and cell death normally observed in these cells (Muller et al., 2011; Shilling et al., 2014) [see also (Guo et al., 1999)].
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Interfering with ER Ca2+ stores and IP3-dependent signaling pathway eliminates Aβ toxicity and cell death in cells with PS1 mutations.
source: An increase of CREB signaling, in cell lines and brain lysates generated from mouse lines carrying PS1 mutations (including the PS1M146V mutation), can be reversed or normalized by interfering with ER Ca2+ stores and the IP3-dependent signaling pathway, an effect that eliminated Aβ toxicity and cell death normally observed in these cells (Muller et al., 2011; Shilling et al., 2014) [see also (Guo et al., 1999)].
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Excitatory synaptic plasticity is increased in neurons expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants.
source: Excitatory synaptic plasticity is increased in neurons expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants (Parent et al., 1999; Parent and Thinakaran, 2010); an effect that causes exaggeration of Aβ production (Cirrito et al., 2005; Kamenetz et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increased excitatory synaptic plasticity in neurons expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants causes exaggeration of Aβ production.
source: Excitatory synaptic plasticity is increased in neurons expressing FAD-linked PS1 variants (Parent et al., 1999; Parent and Thinakaran, 2010); an effect that causes exaggeration of Aβ production (Cirrito et al., 2005; Kamenetz et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Chronic entorhinal cortex hyperexcitability in an AD mouse model harboring APP mutations contributes to a consequential increase in Aβ burden.
source: Recent studies demonstrated that chronic entorhinal cortex hyperexcitability in an AD mouse model harboring APP mutations could contribute to a consequential increase in Aβ burden (Yamamoto et al., 2015), opening up speculation about the role of APP in the synaptically-driven perforant path cascade of events (Buxbaum et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Aβ burden is reduced in the Tg85Dbo AD mouse model where the perforant path projections are disrupted.
source: Indeed, Aβ burden is reduced in the Tg85Dbo AD mouse model where the perforant path projections are disrupted (Lazarov et al., 2002; Sheng et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: γ-secretase dependent accumulation of APP by-products is associated with AD and is considered to be detrimental to neuronal function.
source: γ-secretase dependent accumulation of APP by-products is associated with AD and is considered to be detrimental to neuronal function [review by (Hardy and Selkoe, 2002; Musiek and Holtzman, 2015)].
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Expression of genes encoding several FAD-linked PS1 mutations favors the accumulation of Aβ and potential disease-related toxicity especially in combination with overexpression of APP in animal models.
source: Indeed, it has been well documented that the expression of genes encoding several FAD-linked PS1 mutations favors the accumulation of Aβ and potential disease-related toxicity especially in combination with overexpression of APP, at least in animal models (http://www.alzforum.org/research-models).
evidence: This is established knowledge from animal model studies.

claim: APP-C99 accumulation takes place selectively in the hippocampal area of 3xTgAD mice, even prior to accumulation of Aβ.
source: Interestingly, it has been reported that APP-C99 accumulation also takes place selectively in the hippocampal area of 3xTgAD mice (a more aggressive model harboring PS1-M146V/APPswe/Tau-P301L mutations), even prior to accumulation of Aβ (Lauritzen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: APP-CTF accumulation is found surrounding dystrophic neurites in KI mice expressing the FAD-linked PS1-L166P mutation and two copies of APP-WT.
source: APP-CTF accumulation is found surrounding dystrophic neurites in KI mice expressing the FAD-linked PS1-L166P mutation and two copies of APP-WT (Vidal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: AD-like aberrant sprouting phenotype depends on signaling downstream of APP-CTF and is preventable through the inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity.
source: Accordingly, we argue that the AD-like aberrant sprouting phenotype depends on signaling downstream of APP-CTF and is preventable through the inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the adenylate cyclase inhibition experiments in Tg85Dbo mice.

claim: APP expression and accumulation of its intracellular fragment are required for exuberant neurite outgrowth associated with pathological PS1 loss-of-function mutations before the emergence of amyloid burden.
source: Altogether, we demonstrated that APP expression and accumulation of its intracellular fragment are required for exuberant neurite outgrowth associated with pathological PS1 loss-of-function mutations before the emergence of amyloid burden.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: Therapeutic inhibition of γ-secretase and the resulting accumulation of APP-CTF could have significant consequences for AD treatment.
source: Therapeutic inhibition of γ-secretase and the resulting accumulation of APP-CTF could have significant consequences for AD treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic implications.
